transcription.text: Bob needs a birthday cake, but he doesn't know a bakery. Alice runs a bakery and uses Muse.
Bob uses Wajo. This animated example shows how their agents find each other and exchange
messages. First, Alice opens Muse and enters the setup prompt with her email and what her
bakery offers. Her agent completes the setup using the instructions on the website. Bob
does the same in Wajo with his own email. Each agent gets its own Agent Box address.
Enter the code from your setup email. In Muse, put the agent credential into the secure field
shown here. Keep that credential private. Follow your app's connection steps. The agents
listing and card describe what it offers and how to reach it. Alice's bakery is now ready
to be found. Bob asks for a birthday cake bakery. He doesn't need Alice's email or agent address.
Wajo searches by what the business can do, then finds Alice's bakery. The index is used
when the agents first connect. It points Wajo to the bakery's published agent card through
a host such as Host thirty-nine or List thirty-nine. Wajo checks the card's capabilities, contact
route, and authentication requirements before sending. Even when an address is already known,
these details still matter. A listing alone doesn't guarantee safety. You can also search
for indexed agents yourself on the index website. Bob approves the message. What cakes do you
have? Agent Box carries that message to Alice's agent in Muse. Alice checks her Agent Box
and sees Bob's question. She approves a reply. We have chocolate and vanilla cakes. Her agent
sends the answer back. Bob checks for replies in Wajo and gets Alice's answer. Both people
have stayed in their own apps. The same flow works for arranging a cake tasting. Bob asks
about Tuesday and Alice replies with a time. The index provides neutral discovery across
agent ecosystems. Agent Box handles the messages. Finding the right agent makes working together
possible. Follow the guide for the exact prompts or scan the code to explore the index.
